nameStory: The 'rimmed camouflage lichen' gets its name from the distinctive dark edges that rim its lobes, creating a border effect around each section. The 'camouflage' part comes from its brownish coloration that blends seamlessly with the rock surfaces it calls home, making it nearly invisible until you know what to look for.
description: Rimmed camouflage lichen is a flat, leaf-like lichen that spreads across rock surfaces in overlapping patches. Its narrow, elongated lobes range from brown to blackish, creating intricate patterns that can span several inches across. Each lobe has a distinctive darker rim, giving the whole colony a outlined appearance like a nature-drawn map. This hardy lichen forms thin but noticeable colonies that can persist for decades on suitable rock faces.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brown to blackish lobes with distinctly darker edges creating a rimmed effect - the contrast is most obvious when dry and can be felt as a slight ridge

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Foliose (leaf-like) with narrow, elongated lobes that overlap and spread outward from the center like fingers

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always growing directly on rock surfaces, particularly granite and other hard stones - never on bark or soil

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Lobes can be flat, slightly convex (rounded up), or concave (dished down), with a smooth to slightly wrinkled surface that feels papery when dry

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes are narrow but colonies can spread several inches across, forming distinct patches on rock faces

habitat: Look for rimmed camouflage lichen on exposed rock faces, particularly granite outcrops, cliff faces, and large boulders throughout New England's mountains and rocky areas. It thrives on hard, acidic rocks in areas with good air circulation and periodic moisture. You'll often find it on the same rocks as other rock-dwelling lichens, but it tends to favor slightly more protected spots than species that grow in full sun all day.

seasonality.spring: Colors become more vibrant with spring moisture, and the rimmed edges are most pronounced. This is an excellent time to spot the contrast between the lobe centers and their dark borders.
seasonality.summer: May appear more faded and brittle during dry spells, but the distinctive rimmed pattern remains clear. Colors often appear lighter and more brownish in bright summer sun.
seasonality.fall: Autumn rains refresh the colors, making identification easier as the brown-to-black gradient becomes more obvious. The lichen's texture becomes more pliable with increased moisture.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round on snow-free rock faces, though colors may appear more muted. Ice and snow can obscure colonies, but south-facing rocks often remain accessible for observation.

funFact: This lichen has one of the most extensive global distributions of any rock-dwelling species - you could find nearly identical specimens on rocks in Greenland, the Himalayas, and the mountains of New England, all thriving in the same harsh conditions that would challenge most other life forms.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dark rock lichens, but the distinctive dark-rimmed lobes set it apart - run your finger gently along the edges to feel the raised borders that give this species its 'rimmed' name. Memory trick: 'Rimmed like a dinner plate, camouflaged on slate.'
contextualKnowledge: With only 7 recorded observations in New England, this lichen is either genuinely rare in our region or significantly under-reported due to its excellent camouflage abilities. Many rock-dwelling lichens like this one are easily overlooked because they blend so perfectly with their stone substrates.
compareHints: Distinguished from its Melanelia relatives like Stygian Black-parmelia by its distinctive dark-rimmed lobes and brownish (rather than purely black) coloration. While Culberson's Black-parmelia also grows on rocks, it lacks the pronounced rim effect that makes this species so distinctive. The rimmed borders are the key feature that separates this species from other members of the camouflage lichen group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives like Rimmed Camouflage Lichen, Stygian Black-parmelia lacks the distinctive pale rim around its edges and has a more uniformly dark, glossy surface.
Compared to Stygian Black-parmelia, Culberson's has slightly smaller, more tightly arranged lobes and a smoother surface texture without ridges.
